evidence.claim: Masjid al-Haram currently has 13 minarets (General Presidency statement, 24 Mar 2025).

sources.name: Saudi Press Agency dispatch via UNA-OIC
sources.excerpt: According to the General Presidency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque, the Grand Mosque has 13 minarets, all of which are similar in design but differ in height

evidence.claim: Saudipedia: 'There are thirteen minarets, all of which are similar in their external design.'

sources.name: Saudipedia (official Saudi encyclopedia), Grand Mosque Minarets
sources.excerpt: There are thirteen minarets, all of which are similar in their external design.

evidence.claim: Nine was the genuine historical count after King Fahd's second Saudi expansion (1409 AH / 1988 CE); it later rose to 11 (King Abdullah expansion) and then 13. So '9' is outdated as a current answer but was a real past phase — the question needs a 'currently' qualifier.

sources.name: Journal of Architecture, Planning & Construction Management (IIUM), 'Chronology of Multi Minarets in Mosques'
sources.excerpt: The second expansion of king Fahd Ibn Abdul Aziz 1409/1988 which built new pair minarets on his new entrance ... as a result, the mosque had nine minarets. The third expansion of king Abdullah at present time occurred by building new pair minarets on his entrance, therefore, the mosque has eleven minarets (Holy Mosque, 2013).

evidence.claim: No authentic hadith dates the Isra' and Mi'raj to Rajab or any specific month; every specific dating is unauthenticated per the scholars of hadith.

sources.name: IslamQA.info, fatwa 60288 (quoting Shaykh Ibn Baz)
sources.excerpt: With regard to this night on which the Isra' and Mi'raj took place, there is nothing in the authentic Hadiths to indicate that it is in Rajab or in any other month. Everything that has been narrated concerning a specific date for these events cannot be proven to have come from the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) according to the scholars of Hadith.

evidence.claim: Classical scholarship records five/six differing opinions (Rabi-ul-Awwal, Rabi-u-Thani, Rajab, Ramadan, Shawwal, Zulhijjah); no certainty is possible.

evidence.claim: The Quran's flood narrative (11:40-44) states NO duration — neither for the onset, the flooding, nor the subsiding.

evidence.claim: Tirmidhi 1621: 'The Mujahid is one who strives against his own soul' — graded Hasan Sahih by at-Tirmidhi; also authenticated by al-Hakim and al-Albani (as-Sahihah 549); Ibn Taymiyyah called its isnad jayyid. It defines the mujahid; it does NOT rank any jihad as 'greatest'.

sources.excerpt: The Mujahid is one who strives against his own soul. [Abu 'Eisa said:] ... The Hadith is Hasan Sahih.

evidence.claim: The 'greater jihad' report ('We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad') is not authentic: al-Bayhaqi graded its chain weak; Ibn Hajar traced the wording to the Tabi'i Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah, not the Prophet.

evidence.claim: Shafi'i/Ahmad and the 'preponderant opinion' (Ibn Baz, Permanent Committee) count 15, including both Hajj sajdahs (22:18 and 22:77). The 14-vs-15 differentiator is Hajj 22:77, not Sad 38:24.

note: Keeping both 14 and 15 as correct for near-identical stems is a contradiction. evidence.claim: 540 is the traditional South Asian design goal: 20 rak'ahs x 27 Taraweeh nights = 540 ruku sections, devised by the ulema of Bukhara (~4th century Hijri) to complete the Quran by the 27th of Ramadan.

sources.name: British Library Asian and African Studies Blog (citing 'Abd al-Qayum al-Sindi) + Quran Made Easy (Mufti Afzal Hoosen Elias)
sources.excerpt: As a section of the Qur'an would be recited during each of the 20 rakat (cycles) of the evening tarawih prayers during Ramadan, each concluding with the ordained bow or ruku', the Qur'an was therefore divided into 540 (20 x 27) ruku'

evidence.claim: Actual ruku marker counts are disputed: other authorities give 558, and the Quran Foundation's Indopak-script API models ruku_number up to 558. Rukus are editorial printing markers, not revealed counts.

sources.name: British Library + Quran Foundation API docs
sources.excerpt: although other authorities give the number of ruku' as 558 ... ruku_number ... maximum: 558, minimum: 1

evidence.claim: Al-Hashr 59:22-24 contain only a limited cluster of Allah's names (~15 distinct), not 99. Names present: Allah, Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim (22); Al-Malik, Al-Quddus, As-Salam, Al-Mu'min, Al-Muhaymin, Al-Aziz, Al-Jabbar, Al-Mutakabbir (23); Al-Khaliq, Al-Bari', Al-Musawwir, Al-Hakim (24).

sources.name: Quran.com API (Quran Foundation), 59:22-24, Sahih International
sources.excerpt: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Grantor of Security, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. (59:23)

evidence.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 2736 states Allah has ninety-nine names but lists none of them; no surah is given as the source of a 99-name list.

sources.name: Sunnah.com, Sahih al-Bukhari 2736
sources.excerpt: Allah's Messenger said, 'Allah has ninety-nine names, i.e. one-hundred minus one, and whoever knows them will go to Paradise.'

proposed_fix.question_en: The closing verses of which surah mention several of Allah's names, such as Al-Malik and Al-Quddus?
proposed_fix.question_bn: REVIEW-TRANSLATION: কোন সূরার সমাপনী আয়াতগুলোতে আল্লাহর বেশ কয়েকটি নাম উল্লেখ আছে, যেমন আল-মালিক ও আল-কুদ্দুস?
proposed_fix.explanation_en: Surah Al-Hashr's closing verses (59:22-24) contain a cluster of Allah's names, including Al-Malik (the Sovereign) and Al-Quddus (the Pure). Note: no surah lists all 99 names - the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 2736 says Allah has ninety-nine names but does not list them.
proposed_fix.explanation_bn: REVIEW-TRANSLATION: সূরা আল-হাশরের সমাপনী আয়াতগুলোতে (৫৯:২২–২৪) আল্লাহর বেশ কিছু নাম রয়েছে, যার মধ্যে আল-মালিক ও আল-কুদ্দুস অন্তর্ভুক্ত। মনে রাখুন: কোনো সূরাতেই ৯৯টি নাম একসাথে উল্লেখ নেই — সহীহ বুখারী ২৭৩৬ নম্বর হাদীসে ৯৯টি নামের কথা বলা হলেও নামগুলোর তালিকা দেওয়া হয়নি।
